title: Mobile radiation shielding device for scatter dose reduction during portable radiography in an orthopedic ward
content:
by Jongwat Cheewakul, Natee Ina, Suphalak Khamruang Marshall, Sitthichok Chaichulee

Portable radiography in orthopedic wards exposes healthcare professionals and adjacent patients to scatter radiation in open, shared clinical environments. In crowded wards, maintaining an optimal distance or clearing the area during exposure is often impractical. This study designed, constructed, and evaluated a foldable mobile radiation shielding system comprising two three-panel units, each with a chromed steel frame (210 × 180 cm) with 0.6-mm nominal lead sheets covered by a vinyl outer layer (66 × 100 cm) per panel, mounted on wheeled castors for bedside deployment. The two units were deployed together, one along each lateral side of the bed. Scatter dose rates were measured using an radiation survey meter and a portable X-ray unit during phantom radiography across common orthopedic projections at eight angular positions (0°–315° in 45° increments) and five distances (50–250 cm). The two-unit configuration achieved a median scatter dose reduction of 94.1% (IQR: 88.0%–97.7%; Wilcoxon W = 51,360, N = 320, p < 0.001). Reductions were broadly consistent across tube voltages (65–85 kVp) and remained substantial across all measurement distances (84.3%–89.6% across 50–250 cm), but varied significantly by angular position, with the highest reduction at 90° (mean 96.91%) and the lowest reductions recorded at 0° (mean 54.02%) and 180° (mean 75.69%). These two directions represented the open axial ends of the setup and were not directly covered by the side-mounted shielding panels. Under a representative high-workload scenario, the two-unit configuration reduced estimated annual occupational doses across all projections, with all post-shielding means remaining well below the average annual occupational dose limit of 20 mSv/year. User feedback was more favorable among radiologic technologists (mean 4.80/5) than among orthopedic ward nurses (mean 3.67/5). The two-unit configuration showed substantial scatter reduction and may serve as an additional protective measure during portable radiography in orthopedic ward settings, with positioning guidance required to maximize protection at clinically relevant angular locations.
